landscapes.landscape: Everything this safety net needs already runs on ARM64 Linux with no new download: Docker's own flags make the fence (the OWASP Docker Security Cheat Sheet is the checklist: drop capabilities, no-new-privileges, read-only root, limits, loopback-only ports, never the Docker socket), Tailscale reports its own exposure as JSON (serve status, funnel status, status), and Telegram's Bot API gives a tappable command menu over long polling. Three honest limits on a DGX Spark: Docker's --memory does not hold back GPU memory on GB10's unified memory (NVIDIA forum reports, not official), --storage-opt size needs xfs with pquota so disk has to be measured instead, and Docker publishes ports on every address unless told otherwise, is not filtered by ufw, and its default json-file logs never rotate. For hostile text the research is blunt: "The Attacker Moves Second" (2025) bypassed all twelve published model-side defences it tested, most of them more than 90 percent of the time, and Meta's Rule of Two and Willison's lethal trifecta both say to limit what an agent that reads outside text may do rather than trust a filter. The benchmarks (AgentDojo, InjecAgent, MCPTox for connector tool descriptions) supply attack shapes but score a model inside their own Python environment, not this console's gates, so the release gate should assume the brain obeys the attacker and test the code, which the stand-in fleet's scripted model (test/mock/model.mjs, model-script.json) already allows. In the code most pieces exist but are scattered: the pause, undo_update, the brain restart, the watchdog, sign-ins with end dates, agent keys, the watcher's record of every container's ports and mounts, and a real-brain eval with 16 cases, none hostile. What is missing is a way to use them when the brain is down (chat fails before any words are read), one joined view of what is reachable, and any statement of what is kept: one chat today sits in chats.json, 14 daily copies on Spark 3 and up to 10 install snapshots, and deleting it removes only the first.

landscapes.landscape: Previews are a solved pattern that needs no software on the Sparks: Terraform separates a speculative plan from a saved one and refuses a saved plan once the state has moved; Kubernetes server-side dry run sends the request through the real admission chain and only skips the write; Ansible check mode warns that a module without check support reports nothing and does nothing, and that steps depending on earlier results cannot be previewed; `docker compose --dry-run` exists but plain `docker run` has none, so the console's own plan is the preview. Undo research is just as settled: the compensating-transaction pattern (record each step's undo as it runs, mark points of no return, expect "compensated", not "original state"), Berkeley's GoEx (undo where possible, confine damage where not), and the agent tools' own documents (Claude Code checkpoints do not track shell or outside changes; LangGraph replay re-runs API calls) all say a rewind restores local records, never the outside world. For sandboxes, ToolEmu lets a model pretend to be the tools (68.8% of its findings judged real) and Ansible Molecule converges on throwaway containers; this product already has something stronger, a stand-in fleet that runs the real service against fake docker, curl and hf, and `test/eval.mjs` already puts the real brain on it. In the code today, `deploy_plan`, `cluster_plan` and `where_it_fits` preview only a start of a model already on disk; the job plans again and aborts on an unapproved stop (the stale-plan check, R14); `undo_last_change` reverses one model start or stop from this chat within 24 hours using 50 should-run revisions; `cancel_operation` puts back; `undo_update` restores files but not state. The gaps: twelve of the thirteen changes have no preview, `save_workflow` checks only action names, `run_workflow` leaves earlier steps done when a later one asks or fails, a replaced memory line or saved workflow keeps no previous copy, and the stand-in is a logic sandbox only (starting a model uses no memory there, any model named gemma crashes, and on Linux it reads the real /proc/meminfo). Everything proposed here is Node and bash on ARM64 with no new dependency, container, port or download.

landscapes.landscape: The packaging formats worth borrowing are all plain text in a folder, so they work on ARM64 without a new service: Compose profiles and project names bring a named group of containers up and down, devcontainer.json describes one box (image, mounts, ports, GPU need), Home Assistant blueprints split a shared routine from its local inputs and import by preview, and an Agent Skill is a named folder whose description loads first and whose body loads only when used, a layout that the two coding engines pinned in agentbar/ (opencode and Qwen Code) both document reading. DGX Spark owners already swap recipes as YAML files in git (sparkrun registries and the Spark Arena community registry, Apache-2.0), in a format this console already parses (`fromSparkrun` in service/dig.mjs). NVIDIA's own project packager, AI Workbench (a git repository with .project/spec.yaml that names secrets without values and sets mount sources at run time), has an official DGX Spark playbook, but it is a second control plane with its own service, and a forum thread reports its Hybrid RAG example failing on Spark; Nix reaches the GB10's GPU only through a community flake and a wrapper. The owner's cuVS example is plausible on this hardware (RAPIDS documents aarch64 CUDA 13 packages and NVIDIA ships a CUDA-X Data Science playbook), but there is no cuVS playbook, GB10 support rests on one forum reply that I could not confirm in release notes, and running it needs the Workload block, which is not built. In the product today the parts of a project exist separately and nothing joins them: saved workflows start things but forget what they started (18-workflows.mjs), undo puts back only one chat's last change within a day (20-desired.mjs), the watcher records how every container was started (19-watcher.mjs), and the daily state copy is restored by hand with no test of the restore; there is no export, no project folder and no skill store. So the smallest project that is more than a saved workflow is a saved workflow plus a record of what its last run started and stopped, a folder, and notes loaded only when it is open; it is worth building as two fields and one action on the Procedure block, and not worth a ninth block, a Compose engine or a dev box of its own.

landscapes.landscape: Two of the personal apps run on ARM64 Linux today, but on CPU only: Immich's server, database and machine-learning images are official for arm64 (6 GB minimum by its docs; its CUDA image was still amd64-only in July 2026, and the working GB10 builds are community Dockerfiles that compile ONNX Runtime for 30 to 90 minutes and hold about 9 GB of GPU memory), and Paperless-ngx 3 (July 2026) is arm64 with built-in AI that takes an `openai-like` endpoint, at about 0.8 GB. Frigate is the one that does not fit: its arm64 image is CPU-only (its docs call CPU detection generally not recommended), its NVIDIA paths are amd64 with CUDA 12 or Jetson, I found no GB10 report, and it must watch all day on a GPU while Spark 2's GPU belongs to the brain and Sparks 3 and 4 are powered by hand. Home Assistant 2026.8 ships a built-in integration that points its conversation agent at any OpenAI-compatible URL with a key (vLLM is named), and its speech side is served by small Wyoming containers (Piper has arm64 tags; Parakeet through onnx-asr answers in 0.3 to 0.6 s on old x86 CPUs; faster-whisper has no CUDA on arm64), but Home Assistant itself wants host networking and root, so it belongs on its own small box, not on the hub. For weight: the brain's setup reserves 108 of 128 GB and 8 GB must stay free, which leaves about 12 GB for everything CPU-only on Spark 2; Immich takes roughly 4 to 6 GB while importing, Paperless 1 to 2 GB, two speech containers 2 to 3 GB (third-party figures, to be measured). For reminders the proven pattern is a one-shot timed job delivered to a named chat (OpenClaw's `at` jobs), while syncing a list into the iPhone's Reminders over CalDAV needs another server and its alarms are unverified; in this codebase nothing personal exists yet, but the pieces are close: `remember` and memory.json (20-memory.mjs), the record sent with every owner message (fleetNotes in 19-watcher.mjs), the /v1 gateway with agent keys (15-routes.mjs, 24-handler.mjs), and round one's tell rule, upload tray, search and batch. My read of this owner: the list with reminders and the paper drawer would be used every week, Home Assistant as a caller of the brain is worth an afternoon if the smart plugs arrive through it, Immich and Paperless should stay plain apps the hub merely hosts, and cameras stay off the Sparks.

landscapes.landscape: NVIDIA supports two ways to update a DGX Spark, the DGX Dashboard or five sudo commands ending in a reboot, with no rollback beyond System Repair and System Recovery; what is waiting can be read without sudo on ARM64 (apt-get -s dist-upgrade, /var/run/reboot-required, /etc/dgx-release, nvidia-smi) (https://docs.nvidia.com/dgx/dgx-spark/os-and-component-update.html). The forum record since September 2026 shows why the owner must stay the one who runs them: the 7.5.0 update took about 7 GiB of memory until a kho=off hotfix, 7.6.0 slowed some units, and kernel 7.0.0-1024 (30 October) put units, mostly ones with a display attached, into reboot loops that only a hand at GRUB and an apt-mark hold fixed (forum threads 383222, 383926, 387397). Driver changes also strand engine images: NVIDIA staff confirmed that its vLLM 26.04 image wants driver 595.58 while the Dashboard ships 580.x (thread 379168). For containers, Watchtower was archived on 17 December 2025 and its failures are well recorded (a database carried across major versions, a tag that moved backwards); what works is digest pinning, a registry check without pulling (dockcheck over regctl, Diun), a waiting period for new images (Renovate's minimumReleaseAge) and an update the owner starts. The best field procedure is Petronella's eight-unit GB10 update: record the state first, one canary, verify with a separate read-only script, never power-cycle automatically. The console already holds most of the parts: a registry reader (pinImage), install snapshots with restore.sh, proven-run speeds, and a watcher that records every container's image.

landscapes.landscape: No pipeline runner earns its keep here: Kestra, Windmill, Prefect, Dagster, Temporal, Restate and DBOS each add a server, usually a database, and their own scheduler and secrets, while Make and Snakemake contribute one rule worth copying (a step is done when its output file exists) and OpenClaw's Lobster, the closest agent-side pattern (fixed steps, a halt, a resume token), needs its own gateway and calls its per-item map unreliable. Speech runs on GB10 today: Parakeet TDT 0.6b v3 in a community CUDA 13 container (about 4.7 GB, about 15x real time, files up to 3 hours, the OpenAI path), whisper.cpp large-v3-turbo built for GB10 (1.6 GB), WhisperX patched for Blackwell (24 minutes of audio in 62 seconds with speaker labels, so about 23x, not the 115x round one quoted, in a 15 GB image that needs a Hugging Face token) and NVIDIA's Speech NIMs (5.8 to 25.6 GB offline, with an NGC key); Parakeet's int8 ONNX build does 17 to 30x real time on desktop CPUs, which would make transcription a CPU job on always-on Spark 2, but no ARM64 figure is published. For documents and pictures the product's own catalog (service/catalog.json) already lists what vLLM serves on a Spark: PaddleOCR-VL 1.6, GLM-OCR and Nemotron 3.5 Parse (2 to 3 GB of weights, 7 GB to run), DeepSeek-OCR 2 (12 GB), and vision in both Qwen 3.8 27B (the brain, if its build kept it) and GLM-5.3 Flash; n8n's October write-up measured GLM-OCR at 1.8 seconds a page and Whisper turbo at 0.58 seconds for 30 seconds of audio on one Spark with five other models loaded. Results are checked in practice by cheap code first (numbers in a summary that are not in its source, words per minute, repeated lines, olmOCR's retries and tolerated page error rate) and a model judging only a sample; code cannot prove a summary right. In this codebase a saved workflow (18-workflows.mjs) fails a step that takes over 60 minutes and forgets everything at a restart, operations live in memory (07-jobs.mjs), and round one's run_batch is one prompt over one folder, so nothing yet outlasts Spark 3 and 4 powering down. The smallest pipeline is therefore a saved procedure whose one step is run_batch with up to four file steps and an append-only ledger on disk: Procedure plus Files, with speech and OCR arriving as a Workload and a Way, and no ninth block.
